title: (MC)2: Lazy MemCopy at the Memory Controller
problem: Memory copy operations incur significant CPU overhead due to cache misses that stall the CPU in the critical path. This overhead is especially severe when copied data is sparsely accessed.
motivation: Memory copy is ubiquitous in systems like Protobuf serialization and OS copy-on-write, and reducing its overhead can substantially improve overall performance.
method: When `memcpy` is called, the system does not actually copy the data right away. Instead, it stores a note at the memory controller (the hardware that manages data flow between CPU and main memory) about what data should be copied. Later, when the CPU or cache tries to access that data, the memory controller intercepts the access and performs the copy at that moment. To implement this, the researchers added hardware extensions to the memory controller, introduced a new CPU instruction, and created a software wrapper that makes this deferred approach work exactly like a normal `memcpy` call.
key_novelty: Instead of copying data immediately when `memcpy` is called (causing CPU stalls), the memory controller defers the copy until the data is accessed, eliminating the main source of overhead.
contributions: Lazy memcpy mechanism that defers copying until data access, reducing CPU overhead for sparsely accessed copies
Memory controller extensions to track and asynchronously execute prospective copies
New CPU instruction to expose lazy memcpy functionality
Software wrapper providing backward-compatible memcpy semantics

metrics.other: 250x lower latency on Linux huge page copy-on-write faults

limitations: Limitations not discussed in the abstract.
primary_theme: lazy memory copy at memory controller
